content.body: Imagine you have a sorted list of numbers, but some numbers appear more than once. How can you efficiently remove the duplicates? In this lesson, you'll learn a clever two-pointer technique that solves this in one pass through the array.
content.title: What we'll learn

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
1. Explain why the two-pointer approach works for sorted arrays
2. Implement the removeDuplicates function using two pointers
3. Walk through the algorithm step-by-step with an example
4. Handle edge cases like empty arrays or arrays with no duplicates
content.title: Learning objectives

content.body: Look at this sorted array: [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4]. How would you remove duplicates to get [1, 2, 3, 4]? Think about how you might do this manually. What's your first instinct?
content.title: Try it

content.body: Now consider a much larger sorted array with 10,000 elements. If you tried to check every element against every other element, that would be very slow. How could you take advantage of the fact that the array is sorted?
content.title: Think about efficiency

content.body: You probably thought about comparing adjacent elements or keeping track of what you've seen. That's good intuition! The key insight is that in a sorted array, duplicates always appear next to each other.
content.title: What you considered

steps.phase: Why we need a better method
steps.title: Why we need a better method

content.body: Checking every possible pair would take too long for large arrays. We need an approach that only goes through the array once. The solution involves using two pointers to track positions as we move through the sorted list.
content.title: Why we need a better method

content.body: Think of this like having two markers in your array. One marker keeps track of where to place the next unique element, while the other scans through the array looking for new unique values. Since the array is sorted, whenever we find a value different from what we last placed, we know it's unique.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Imagine two friends walking through a sorted line of people. One friend points to where the next unique person should stand, while the other scans ahead to find people who look different from the last one placed.

content.body: We'll use two pointers: one (let's call it 'write') tracks where to write the next unique element, and another ('read') scans through the array. When nums[read] is different from nums[write], we've found a new unique value, so we move it to position write+1 and advance both pointers.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. If the array is empty, return 0
2. Initialize write pointer at index 0
3. Loop through array with read pointer starting at index 1
4. If current element is different from element at write pointer:
   - Advance write pointer
   - Copy current element to write position
5. Return write + 1 (number of unique elements)

content.body:
Congratulations! You've implemented an efficient solution to remove duplicates from a sorted array. Remember:
1. The two-pointer approach works because the array is sorted (duplicates are adjacent)
2. The write pointer tracks where to place the next unique element
3. We return write + 1 because write is an index (0-based) but we need the count
4. This solution runs in O(n) time and uses O(1) extra space
